3. Exporting data

Source: vignettes/articles/33_Exporting_data.Rmd
33_Exporting_data.Rmd

Data in CFDataset or CFVariable instances can be exported to several other formats for further processing. The examples below use a data set included with the package:

library(ncdfCF)
  
# Get a netCDF file, here hourly data for 2016-01-01 over Rwanda
fn <- system.file("extdata", "ERA5land_Rwanda_20160101.nc", package = "ncdfCF")
  
# Open the file and get a variable from the data set
ds <- open_ncdf(fn)
t2m <- ds[["t2m"]]

If you would like to see other export formats supported, please open an issue or, better yet, provide the code through a PR.

Exporting to a data.table

A CFVariable can be converted to a data.table which will turn every element in the CFVariable data array into a row in the data.table. The axes of the CFVariable will become columns in the data.table. Two attributes are added to the data.table: name indicates the long name of the CFVariable, units indicates the physical unit of the data values. Other attributes of the CFVariable are not preserved.

# install.packages("data.table")
library(data.table)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'data.table'
#> The following object is masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     %notin%
head(t2m$data.table())
#>    longitude latitude                time      t2m
#>        <num>    <num>              <char>    <num>
#> 1:      28.0       -1 2016-01-01T00:00:00 293.8875
#> 2:      28.1       -1 2016-01-01T00:00:00 294.4015
#> 3:      28.2       -1 2016-01-01T00:00:00 294.4972
#> 4:      28.3       -1 2016-01-01T00:00:00 293.9426
#> 5:      28.4       -1 2016-01-01T00:00:00 293.6339
#> 6:      28.5       -1 2016-01-01T00:00:00 293.0206

The CFVariable$profile() method can produce a data.table directly, avoiding the intermediate step of producing a new CFVariable.

rwa <- t2m$profile(longitude = c(30.07, 30.07, 29.74), latitude = c(-1.94, -1.58, -2.60), 
                   .names = c("Kigali", "Byumba", "Butare"), .as_table = TRUE)
head(rwa)
#>    longitude latitude                time .variable   .value
#>        <num>    <num>              <char>    <char>    <num>
#> 1:     30.07    -1.94 2016-01-01T00:00:00    Kigali 290.4055
#> 2:     30.07    -1.94 2016-01-01T01:00:00    Kigali 290.0088
#> 3:     30.07    -1.94 2016-01-01T02:00:00    Kigali 289.3608
#> 4:     30.07    -1.94 2016-01-01T03:00:00    Kigali 288.8414
#> 5:     30.07    -1.94 2016-01-01T04:00:00    Kigali 288.4713
#> 6:     30.07    -1.94 2016-01-01T05:00:00    Kigali 289.9276
attr(rwa, "value")
#> $name
#> [1] "2 metre temperature"
#> 
#> $unit
#> [1] "K"

Exporting to terra or stars

Packages terra and stars are widely used in the R community for their versatility in working with geospatial data. It should be noted that they both have a very narrow concept of the coordinate system of data variables. In neither package is it possible to store attributes with the axes, for instance, and they do not support important CF features like boundaries around coordinate values, model calendars, auxiliary latitude-longitude grids, auxiliary coordinate labels, scalar axes or parametric vertical coordinates. They do support significant spatial analysis features, including coordinate transformations, that can be very useful when analysing multi-dimensional data, which is why the export functions are included in this package.

A CFVariable can be exported to a terra::SpatRaster (3D) or terra::SpatRasterDataset (4D), depending on the number of axes in the CFVariable.

#install.packages("terra")
suppressMessages(library(terra))
t2m$terra()
#> class       : SpatRaster
#> size        : 21, 31, 24  (nrow, ncol, nlyr)
#> resolution  : 0.1, 0.1  (x, y)
#> extent      : 27.95, 31.05, -3.05, -0.95  (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax)
#> coord. ref. : 
#> source(s)   : memory
#> names       : 2016-~00:00, 2016-~00:00, 2016-~00:00, 2016-~00:00, 2016-~00:00, 2016-~00:00, ...
#> min values  :  284.288049,  284.124237,  283.655365,  283.282614,  283.018168,  283.751937, ...
#> max values  :  296.313559,  294.994941,  294.432655,  294.589247,  293.936255,  294.377149, ...

The function to export a CFVariable or a CFDataset with multiple variables to a stars object is included in the stars package. No attributes from the CF object(s) will be preserved.

# install.packages("stars")
suppressMessages(library(stars))
st_as_stars(t2m)
#> stars object with 3 dimensions and 1 attribute
#> attribute(s):
#>             Min.  1st Qu.   Median    Mean  3rd Qu.     Max.
#> t2m [K] 283.0182 291.1691 293.6186 293.642 296.2347 302.0447
#> dimension(s):
#>           from to         offset   delta    refsys x/y
#> longitude    1 31          27.95     0.1 OGC:CRS84 [x]
#> latitude     1 21          -0.95    -0.1 OGC:CRS84 [y]
#> time         1 24 2016-01-01 UTC 1 hours   POSIXct

Exporting to zarr or geozarr

Zarr is a storage format for n-dimensional data that is optimised for use over the internet or through the cloud, although it may also be used efficiently on a local file system. Data is stored in a Zarr store, a hierarchical structure of groups and arrays. GeoZarr is a set of community conventions for describing geospatial data in Zarr stores. The combination of Zarr and GeoZarr is comparable to netCDF and CF Metadata conventions.

The zarr package is a R-native implementation of the Zarr specification and the geozarr package implements the GeoZarr conventions. In combination they can ingest netCDF data while preserving the semantic meaning of the CF conventions, although in a different encoding. This package allows you to save an entire CFDataset or a single CFVariable to a Zarr store.

z <- ds$geozarr()
z
#> ── Zarr ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ── Memory store - version 3 ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ✔ Listing ✔ Writing ✔ Deleting ✖ Consolidated metadata
#> ── Contents ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ℹ Arrays: 4
#> ── Attributes ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> • Conventions: CF-1.6
#> • history: Attributes simplified for example.
z$hierarchy()
#> ── Zarr hierarchy  ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#> ☰ / (root group)
#>   ☰ coordinates
#>     ⌗ longitude [float32] [31]
#>   ⌖ t2m [float64] [longitude = 31, latitude = 21, time = 24]
#>   ⌖ pev [float64] [longitude = 31, latitude = 21, time = 24]
#>   ⌖ tp [float64] [longitude = 31, latitude = 21, time = 24]

Aggregating netCDF data

NetCDF files have size limitations, due to limitations in various file system drivers. Most netCDF files that are published for wide-scale distribution are therefore limited to about 2GB. For CMIP6 data and other large data sets this implies that a single run of data is broken up into multiple netCDF files. That leads to problems during analysis: separate chunks of data from multiple files have to be stitched together again.

Zarr stores do not have the same size limitation; stores are effectively boundless in size because a single data set is broken up into multiple chunks and reassembled before presenting it back to the user, all behind-the-scenes.

The aggregate_geozarr() function of this package allows you to aggregate multiple compatible netCDF files into a single Zarr store, such as the 3 to 16 netCDF files that make up a single daily run of CMIP6 data. While the aggregation can take place over any axes (with the exception of parametric vertical axes), aggregating over the temporal dimension is the most common pattern.

# Not run dynamically: CMIP6 data used here is 3GB+ in size

# Get a list of compatible files, here 4 CMIP6 daily ACCESS-CM2 data for precipitation
> fn <- list.files(path = "~/my_data/CMIP6/day", pattern = "^pr_day_ACCESS-CM2", full.names = TRUE)

# Create a Zarr store to hold the data, with a group for the data variable
> z <- zarr::create_zarr("~/ACCESS-CM.zarr")
> grp <- z$add_group("/", "variables")

# Aggregate the netCDF data from the 4 files in a single Zarr array
> gza <- aggregate_geozarr(fn, grp)
Opening file 1 of 4: pr_day_ACCESS-CM2_ssp245_r1i1p1f1_gn_20150101-20391003_v20191108.nc
Opening file 2 of 4: pr_day_ACCESS-CM2_ssp245_r1i1p1f1_gn_20391004-20640705_v20191108.nc

Supported features

The zarr and geozarr packages do not fully support all CF constructs. The CF constructs supported by ncdfCF can all be exported successfully to geozarr, with some caveats.

  • All coordinate system constructs are exported to geozarr, including auxiliary lat-long grids. Support for parametric vertical coordinates will be added in the near future. For regularly-spaced coordinates no separate Zarr arrays (like coordinate variables in netCDF) are created - the values are compressed and stored inline with the attributes of the referring data variable.
  • All attributes are exported, including global attributes and group attributes. Attributes that contain structural information for netCDF encoding, like “coordinates” or scale/offset, are not copied. Attributes that denote valid data are handled separately - see next section. The “history” attribute is converted to a JSON array.
  • Referenced objects, like ancillary variables and external variables (when data is linked), must be exported separately. geozarr currently has no mechanism to establish the linkages between objects, but the CF attributes establishing these linkages are copied over.

Discrete sampling geometries are currently not supported in geozarr.

Handling missing data

CF-encoded netCDF files describe missing data with a handful of overlapping attributes: _FillValue, missing_value, valid_min, valid_max and valid_range. Zarr has a single, narrowly defined concept: the fill_value of an array indicates data that has never been written. When data are copied from CF variables to GeoZarr arrays, for instance with copy_to_geozarr() or CFVariable$write_geozarr(), the CF attributes for missing data are translated into a small, unambiguous encoding. This section describes that translation.

Principle

The Zarr fill_value is never derived from CF attributes. It always has the Zarr default for the data type of the array and it means one thing only: the element has never been written. For the numeric types the default values are the same as the netCDF library default fill values, except for 64-bit integers.

Cells that were written but are missing are encoded separately, with an optional missing_value attribute on the array. A reader of the Zarr store that wants to find all missing data must therefore honour both the fill_value and the missing_value attribute. The zarr and geozarr packages apply the fill_value only.

What is read from the CF file

Data are read through package RNetCDF, which sets cells to NA that are equal to the _FillValue or missing_value attributes, or that are outside the valid range. Packed data are checked for validity before they are unpacked, as the CF Conventions (section 2.5.1) require. The data that are copied therefore have NA for every missing cell, regardless of how the producer encoded it.

Translation rules

The rules apply to every data variable and to auxiliary coordinate variables, but not to character variables, for which no attributes are set.

  • The fill_value of the Zarr array is the Zarr default for its data type.
  • The missing_value of the Zarr array is a single value that is determined as follows. A packed variable (with a scale_factor or add_offset) has none: the sentinel belongs to the packed encoding and CF prescribes that it is not transformed, so missing cells are NA in the unpacked data. Otherwise, if the variable has a missing_value attribute, its first element is used. Otherwise, if the variable has a _FillValue that is different from the netCDF library default for the data type, that value is used. A _FillValue that equals the library default does not denote missing data, it merely repeats the default. If none of these apply there is no missing_value.
  • If there is a missing_value, then every NA in the data is written as that value. Several sentinels in the source, such as a vector missing_value or a missing_value and a different _FillValue, are thus collapsed into one. If there is no missing_value then NA is written as the fill_value.
  • The valid_range of the Zarr array is a vector of two values, in unpacked units. The valid_range attribute takes precedence over valid_min and valid_max. When only one of the latter is present, the other bound is the largest finite double. For packed variables the bounds are unpacked and put in increasing order. The range is recorded for documentation: the data have already been masked by it when they are read.
  • No other CF attributes for missing data are written. In particular _FillValue, valid_min, valid_max and valid_range are not carried over.

State of the cells

After conversion every cell of the Zarr array is in one of three states:

  1. Valid data.
  2. Written but missing: the cell holds the missing_value, or the fill_value if the array has no missing_value.
  3. Never written, for instance in a part of the array that is not covered by any of the aggregated files: the cell holds the fill_value.

Caveats

  • A real value in the data that is equal to the fill_value is read as NA by the zarr package. A real NaN in the source data is treated as missing and is written as the missing_value or the fill_value.
  • The comparison with the netCDF library default fill value is done on double values with a small tolerance. For 64-bit integer data types this is approximate, which is sufficient to recognise the default.
  • When data from multiple netCDF files are copied into one Zarr array, the missing_value and valid_range attributes are set again for each file and the last one wins. The files are assumed to be consistent, as they would be when produced by a single producer.
